content:
Hold on to the last moment

"To be honest, I held on until the last moment." The two sisters grew up in Wang Fuk Court with their parents. After their father passed away and the elder sister got married, Ms Yuen lived with her mother until the fire. Her mother died in the blaze. During the period of going upstairs, she once wore a sweater with the words "rebuild on the original site" handwritten on it to express her demands. But the authorities rejected it and the owners' committee refused to discuss it. It was not until a week before the acquisition deadline of 31 August that she submitted a "letter accepting the acquisition proposal".

Ms Yuen believes that Wang Fuk Court residents have already been "trapped with no way out". She said that the two explainers she had come into contact with in the past were unable to answer her questions, and their only clear goal was to press residents on whether they had sold their flats.

Post-disaster life is "temporary lodging"

Since the fire, Ms Yuen has stayed at Shin Lau in Tai Po, and later moved to Yue Ying Lau in Aberdeen, paying a "temporary residence fee" each month. The bed, dining table and TV cabinet that originally existed in the unit, as well as the neighbours and security guard, all served as reminders of her status. She described her life after the incident as "temporary lodging".

Reflecting on what "home" and "house" mean

She returns to this empty unit at eight or nine o'clock every day after work, and on holidays chooses to leave and go to her sister's home. "In fact, after the incident, I have already started thinking about what is called a 'home', what is called a 'house'. A home is supposed to be a safe place, but when this home in Wang Fuk Court can be burned down by someone..."

"Now the word 'home' is quite heavy for me"

When the reporter asked Ms Yuen about her vision of home, she said the old phone containing photos of Wang Fuk Court was also lost in the fire, and all the fragments remain only in her memory. She sighed deeply: "(Home) is not just about having a bed, a cabinet, a bedroom, and a full range of home appliances given to me, and that makes it a so-called proper home. It made me rethink what the elements of a proper home are, so I can't answer this question for now, because now the word 'home' is quite heavy for me."

Dissatisfied with officials' "letting go" rhetoric

The responses of senior officials to the Wang Fuk Court fire, such as Deputy Chief Secretary Cheuk Wing-hing's remarks on "letting go" and Financial Secretary Deputy Wong Wai-lun's talk about market value, have continually accumulated her helplessness and anger. "The more silent you are, the less I understand," she said. "When they can actually say such callous things, what do they really think about the meaning of home?"

A sense of being "sold off cheaply"

Recalling the moment she signed the letter accepting the acquisition, Ms Yuen said the strongest feeling was one of unwillingness and "indignation", a sense of being "sold off cheaply", because home is not only about monetary value but also about emotional and memory connections. "The flat was something my father and mother worked so hard for. If it really has to be taken from us for nothing, I am even more unwilling than simply feeling that it is being 'sold off cheaply' now."

After signing the letter, Ms Yuen will lose her status as an owner. The independent committee has postponed the submission of its report until October. Ms Yuen said that holding those responsible accountable is part of it, "but how I end this personally, I cannot answer. Because from the incident until now, life feels like a total loss. First, home was burned down, and what burning it down means is that it seems to have erased the history of my growing up. A family member also died in the fire, and it was a sudden death... there is a huge hole in my heart. Can this hole really be filled? Or can it one day heal? I don't know how to answer."
